utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We won't be long. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Karnavas: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, when we left off, we were talking about the 17th, and I just wanted to finish off the questions in that area before we move on. You told us what you had done in Bratunac, and then that you went back to Han Pijesak. Could you please tell us whether you made any reports as a result of the tasks that had been given to you by General Mladic, written or oral?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In writing, I did not receive anything. That's for sure. Orally, I conveyed what I saw at the operation centre of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, aside from that task, did you have any other involvement on any activities related to Srebrenica? And we're talking about the events in Srebrenica after its fall of July 11th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to go back to -- well, since you -- in light of your answer, let me just go into another area. Have you been engaged at all in any commissions or fact-finding missions with respect to what occurred in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you've noticed, in response to one of your previous questions, I said that I learned more from the past year when work was done in Republika Srpska on revealing the truth concerning Srebrenica and in relation to the Chamber of Human Rights with regard to that particular matter. So in these activities, I did take part, and I still take part in them, but not as a member of the commission. But as a member of the Ministry of Defence, which as an institution is charged with certain tasks by the commission. Each and every one of us within the scope our possibilities, tasks, and duties is trained to do their best.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us a little bit about what you specifically do in relation to this commission. You told us you're not a member. But what is the level of your participation or activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security administration, or rather, the security service of defence which organisationally belongs to the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, together with all the other parts of the system of defence, that is to say, the Army of Republika Srpska, the General Staff and its units, the administration for legal matters. I think those are all the parts of the Ministry of Defence that respond to inquiries made by the commission that is working on the decision of the Chamber on Human Rights in relation to the Srebrenica case. The service that I head does what it can do. Within the system of defence, it collects information related to these events. So that is what we have been dealing with over the past several months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In relation to the information that your ministry collects, could you please tell us what sort of information is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the decision of the Chamber on Human Rights specifically calls upon the Government of Republika Srpska to give answers to certain questions. I cannot exactly quote the decision and all the requests contained in it, but the key question in that decision is that questions related to the fate of the people from Srebrenica between the 10th and 19th of July 1995 should be answered; that is to say, that the fate of these people is the key question that has to be answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So to the extent that the Ministry of Defence may have data in their archives, is that the sort of data that you would provide to the commission if and when they request such data?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of an investigation this commission is doing or how they go about in their investigation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. The commission on the basis of the authority vested in it by the government of Republika Srpska by virtue of its very establishment initiated a great many activities, and it has been working in several directions. Among others, it includes the following: One team from the commission consisting of members of the commission deals with archives in the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of the Interior, the Intelligence Security Agency, the judiciary, or rather all archives from that period of time. Another group collects information, or rather interviews some of the participants in the events in and around Srebrenica. Another group analyses the material that is accessible and that was compiled either by the representatives of the international community or various commissions, experts, et cetera. So all these findings are contained among that material. This group studies everything that is accessible and that has been proven so far through the work of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, that is to say, this Tribunal. So all of that is critically analysed and viewed and taken as a point of departure for further efforts made along those lines. That is my understanding of what this commission does. They bring all of this together, and then submit their preliminary reports. Very shortly, they are due to present their final report concerning these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it in light of your answer that the one team that examines all this documentation or analyses it, that would include statements by accused who have entered agreements with the Prosecution and have testified based on the agreements and benefits that they derive from such agreements?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not your task, is it? You're not included in that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, no. Although I did have the opportunity to look through a considerable portion of this material. As a matter of fact, I even used it as a basis for some activities in that direction in order to gain reliable knowledge about these events faster and more efficiently. I'm sorry, I have to add something to the previous answer I gave. A very important institute, or rather, a very important way in which the commission works is the introduction of the institute of a protected witness. I believe that this is the first thing that made it possible to make major headway in this direction. So that is how the commission has been working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The way I understand it, if I'm correct, and what I've read in the press recently, the high representative was rather critical of the pace and perhaps even the work of the commission. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that. His assessment was, and he made a decision along those lines; namely, his assessment was that the commission was not working properly. It was dealing with questions that were not part of the essence of the decision involved. He also assessed that things were moving very slowly, and he adopted a few measures including personnel changes within the commission itself. That is to say, the chairman of the commission was removed, replaced, and the chief of general staff was removed because, as he had put it, the non-possession of the war archives of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I believe that's all I have with respect to that topic. And I just want to cover one last detail. If I could direct your attention again, please, to Exhibit P389. And this was an exhibit that we looked at yesterday, the instruction dated 24 October 1994, if you could look at that. First of all, who signed this instruction? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signator is the signature of General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was for General Mladic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that General Tolimir was your superior officer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir was the second in the line of command, or rather, he was head of the sector for intelligence and security affairs and assistant commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And yesterday, you told us that you don't recall seeing this instruction. And I failed to ask you how is it if you were working in the security sector at that point in time in history, that is, 1994, how is it possible that you did not see this instruction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to that sector in the month of February 1995. That is to say, that in the preceding period, I was not in the security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, just one other minor point or detail, in looking at this instruction, I would like you to -- I will like to direct your attention to paragraph number 2. And if you could tell us, based on this instruction which I also believe you indicated is fundamentally based on the existing laws and regulations of the VRS, could you please tell us what other laws one would need to be acquainted with in order to fully understand and appreciate this instruction, in particular, paragraph 2? The full paragraph, that is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many laws, regulations, and directions, but I will try to list the most important ones. The law on the State Security Service, the law on the interior, the law on Criminal Procedure, the Criminal Code, the law on defence, the law on the military, those are the key laws. In addition to that, there are rules, rules of service in the security organs, rules of service of the military police, directions for the combined application of methods of work, directions on methods of work in the security organs, directions on the application of rules in the military police, directions on the work of security organs during exercises, during imminent threat of war and in wartime, and other individual sets of directions. Those are the key documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether chief of security and intelligence sectors or organs at the bringing levels, did they all have the requisite knowledge and training on these laws in order to understand the application of this instruction, particularly as it relates to the function with respect to counter-intelligence activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not all. The security organs from the previous state, from the previous army who assumed their duties after initial training or after having completed appropriate courses and after being appointed to certain positions, they were familiar with all of this and they knew it for the most part. To a lesser extent and with variations from one individual to another, this was something that the security organs were aware of as the Army of Republika Srpska grew. At that time, it was the armed people, the concept of the armed people that was prevalent, and then it grew into the Army of Republika Srpska. They worked and trained themselves. And through such instructions, they were gradually trained and educated. If one looks at the overall staff in that service, it would be hard to say which percentage was involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question: Yesterday I believe you indicated that you were not acquainted with Momir Nikolic back in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it begs the next question, which is how is it that you being a member of the security organ at the Main Staff, albeit you had your own specialty there, how is it that you didn't know someone the likes of Captain Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply it was not only Momir Nikolic who was a security organ that I did not know. There must have been tens of members of the service, or perhaps even more, whom I did not know. This was a big wartime army, and there were many members of the service in it, too. I was really not involved in these personnel matters. So quite simply, with the exception of the units that I served on and adjacent units, I did not know people who served as security organs. At that time, I did not even know the chief of security of the Drina Corps, Popovic. I met him only later. I met him because he -- I actually knew Colonel Tomic, his predecessor, who had come from Banja Luka and he was a security organ in the previous army, too [as interpreted]. But persons who had joined the service during the war from the reserve force, people I did not have any contact with before the war and who served in areas where I simply was not, I did not know them and I had no way of knowing them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I want to thank you very much for being frank and forthcoming in all of your answers. I'm sure there will be some questions by perhaps Mr. Stojanovic, the Prosecution, and the Judges. If you could be equally as forthcoming and forthright with them, I would most appreciate it. Again, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please kind enough to help us with respect to the implementation of the regulations governing the activities of the security service. According to those rules of service, do security organs in the brigade have the duty to be on-duty operations officers in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that a little. Why is it so that security officers as a rule have no obligations to keep duty service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security service has its own system of duty which means that they are on duty, that is, duty service is organised on the basis of garrisons, or in wartime, at the level of the corps. When the security organs from the corps units and corps departments take turns being on duty 24 hours, that is, round the clock, without an assistant, which means that they are alone round the clock, and they must be available to the duty officer at the superior level of the security service. That is how it is regulated by the rules. And during that duty service, the security organ does not take part. That is at the operations level of duty service in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that assistant commanders for security in the brigades were well aware of those rules.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible for a security officer, because of the needs of the service, to leave the area of his brigade and to cross over to another brigade without his commander knowing it, for this to be done without the commander being aware of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the rule. He may leave, but he must tell the commander that he's outside the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If my understanding of your answer is correct, this means I don't have to ask the commander for permission or approval, but I have to inform the commander that I have left the area of defence of my brigade and crossed over to the area of another brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That I am leaving the area, so I must inform the commander before I leave that I am leaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me also add, if a security officer is given instructions to travel beyond the zone of defence of his brigade, does he again need to have approval of the commander to travel to Yugoslavia or somewhere else outside the zone of defence of his brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean "travel to Yugoslavia." If you mean any kind of travel, then it is normal and it is the rule for the commander to know about it. And the commander will assess whether that is necessary or not. And anyway, the commander will have to participate in deciding whether such travel is necessary or does it affect his duties? So the commander must grant him approval to make a trip of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if because of the needs of his own activities he goes to the area of responsibility of another brigade, he has to inform his commander before doing that. Could I now ask the usher to assist us in showing the witness a document. It is the text of the statement of facts when Dragan Obrenovic pleaded guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary, Your Honours, we have this statement in English should it be necessary for you to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's customary that we have an English copy so we can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, I think we have already mentioned that before, if you are going to use a document in your direct examination or cross-examination, especially in the direct examination, you have to inform the Chamber and the other parties beforehand so that we could be prepared in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. That is my omission. I thought that this was a text that has been published long ago. It is not really an exhibit, nor do we intend to tender it into evidence. I just wanted to use this statement for the witness to assess -- assist us with the rules of service. But certainly, in future even in such situations, we will provide the information on time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, could we please jointly have a look at paragraph 5 and 6 of the statement of facts. It is 5 and 6 in the English, too, in which it says -- it is a statement by Dragan Obrenovic in which he acknowledges that he was in command of the Zvornik Brigade during the absence of Commander Vinko Pandurevic until his return at about midday on the 15th of July. And then he says: "On hearing of this plan to kill the prisoners, I as acting commander took responsibility for the plan and supported the implementation of this plan." In the next paragraph, he says: "Then I decided to send a commander of the military police company and five military policemen to assist him." My question would be in view of what you told us yesterday regarding the rules of service, under the concept of "supported the implementation of this plan," does that imply that there must have been an order on the use of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand what he meant when he said this. But if this was the assignment, then certainly the company commander must have been issued such a task. We see from this that he was in command of the brigade and that he has the right to issue orders to the company commander. But that is not your question. Mija Mirasekovic [phoen] who is mentioned as the company commander, regardless of Obrenovic's order had the right and duty not to carry out such an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for him to be used, the order of the commander was indispensable.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point yesterday, you said in answer to a question by Mr. Karnavas that you never were told by Beara and Popovic what they had been doing during those days. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question would be, security officers such as the chief of the security service in the Main Staff, Mr. Ljubisa Beara, and the assistant commander for security in the Drina Corps, Mr. Popovic, should they, according to the rules, report to the duty operations officer in the Zvornik Brigade about their activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the duty officer in the Zvornik Brigade, they should not report. They have no legal obligation to report to such a duty officer. But they do have the duty and obligation to report to their corps commander about what they were doing. That would apply to Popovic. And Beara would have to report to General Tolimir as his superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that a duty officer in an infantry brigade is not the level to which they should report to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. Your Honour, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes cross-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, could we move the machine. Cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They have the ability to make it go down. That's okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly where we left off, if Colonel Beara or Popovic or a senior security person like that came to a brigade with a specific job that he'd been ordered to do by his commander that involved prisoners and guarding of prisoners and various assets and troops from that brigade and other areas, would it be normal for him to check in with the duty officer and get his assistance in communicating with the different units he might need to help him organise the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. My objection is the complexity of the question. I think it would be more correct in accordance with the Rules to rephrase the question. If there are no other superior officers, when they are there or when they are not there, then the duty officer. That is my impression, that that is how the question should be phrased. In this way, the possibility's open whether they should contact and ask the duty officer. We don't know whether the superior's there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think you gave some hints to the witness for the answer. This is a cross-examination, and the Prosecutor could ask any questions they like if they are relevant. First, I believe this question is relevant to your question; secondly, there should be -- I think the follow-up questions on this. We'll see the witness's answer first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. The Defence attorney responded, but my answer really would have been anyway that the duty officer in the unit at any level can deal with certain matters only in the absence of the actual commander or the person who is by establishment replacing him in that position or through some other measure is standing in for him. The duty officer may address certain matters. But he cannot take upon himself the role of command of the unit fully. He cannot fully replace the commander, nor can he decide on the use of the unit. For this, he has to get the approval of the commander for each and every operation that he intends to carry out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. I think we understand the duty officer is not the commander unless all the commanders are absent, and then he is the one that gets stuck with that responsibility. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When a person contacts the brigade by phone or communication, that generally goes into the duty officer office. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the line of duty service, yes. But according to the chain of command, the commander would be the person that would be asked for first. So it follows the line of subordination. If questions have to do with the functioning of the duty service itself, that is, the tasks provided for in the instructions for the duty officer, then yes. But it is not right to say that one has to contact the duty officer first in each and every occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So for example, if you're a general and you need to contact directly a brigade, you would probably prefer to speak to the brigade commander first if he's in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or the deputy commander if the commander's not in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am using the communications devices or radio connections or relay connections, whichever, in most cases I would call up the person I needed. If I'm coming in person to the unit, to the command post, at the first barrier, at the gate, I will announce my presence through the soldier at the reception desk that I wish to see the commander, the Chief of Staff, the chief of security, the chief of artillery, whoever it is I wish to visit. And then the technical matters are taken care of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking about when you telephone in. When you telephone in, you would want to speak to the commander first; if he's not available, it would be the deputy commander. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you're communicating directly with the duty officer, that may be some indication that the commander and the deputy commander were not available. Is that a fair inference? You as a general calling in to a brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's briefly go back to a bit of your discussion on some of the rules. You, of course, concentrated on the security rules. And I want to take you to the situation specifically of the rules and structures of the light infantry brigade. And in the light infantry brigade, am I correct to say that the jobs of the intel officer and the security officer are one and the same, held by the same person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the rules, it says "brigade," and then in brackets, infantry, armoured, mechanised, light, mountain, et cetera. All the different types of brigade are listed. So the brigade is a unit of the army of combined and variable composition, "variable" is the key word here. It is possible that a light infantry brigade may have one person performing both those functions; that is, both intelligence and security. But in such a light brigade, which is by formation equivalent to a battalion, then there are two or more persons sharing those duties, and then a department for intelligence and security is set up which has a chief and an assistant in charge of the intelligence. It is not identical in all units, but in a specific unit it is possible for one person to be performing both those functions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those rules can be adapted to fit the situation of the particular brigade I would take it, within reason.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that at the time in the July 1995, the Bratunac Brigade had one person that was covering both intel and security?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time, I didn't know how this was resolved in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, then let's just assume that that's the way it was. And I just want to ask you a couple of questions. If we do have a brigade person that's covering both intel and security, does the intel person have the same discretion in receiving combat intel information not to tell his commander if he so chooses that he would in counter-intelligence information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- to interrupt, but he's talking about intelligence and counter-intelligence. I don't believe there's any testimony that the intelligence officers are dealing with counter-intelligence information. I don't know whether Mr. McCloskey misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This is a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, but it has to be based on facts. You can't have an intel officer dealing with counter-intelligence, albeit he has got a split personality, you know, in a sense, that he's carrying two hats at the same time, but -- very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, sometimes these things happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The officer is in charge of counter-intelligence and he's in charge of combat intelligence, the person that's wearing both hats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is, is when this officer receives combat intelligence information from a source, does he have the discretion that we have learned about from Prosecution witnesses and Defence witnesses, does he have that discretion not to inform his commander of combat intelligence that he has in some situations as you've described in counter-intelligence information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer that question even though perhaps I'm not the best person for doing so. But what is quite beyond doubt is that the intelligence service is a staff service. As for intelligence combat information, the organ, regardless of whether those two functions are combined in one person or not, he cannot keep quiet about anything and not tell his Chief of Staff or commander. He doesn't have the right to select intelligence information and keep something to himself without informing his superior command. So that service is always linked to the Chief of Staff or the deputy commander. But anyway, that is the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And now getting to the security officer and this division which I think you said was two-thirds counter-intelligence, one-third investigation, military-police-type work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security service, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the side of it that's mentioned in this document 389A, the one Tolimir issued the instructions on this, that you've seen, I don't think we need -- it says: "The remaining 20 per cent of their engagement consist of administrative and staff, military police and criminal legal tasks and duties." So tasks involving the military police don't come under the counter-intelligence side of things. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And counter-intelligence, just to try to get a little better feel for what this might be, we saw a document which I don't think we need to bring out, but where the chief of security sent it to the -- of the corps sent it to the chief of security in the brigades secretly, and it had to do with a plot on Mladic's life. And is that the kind of counter-intelligence that needs to be kept secret so that it can be sorted out and resolved most effectively?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why if we're talking about General Mladic, I really can't explain why this would go towards the brigades. In any event, it should have gone in the direction of the sector for intelligence and security affairs of the Main Staff. I'm afraid the question is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe it went there as well. But I'm just -- a plot on the commander from within perhaps his own command, is that the kind of thing we might keep commanders on the ground out of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such an event, there would have to be an assessment as to which commander should be informed about it and to what extent. So it could come under the area of counter-intelligence, highly specialised security activities. Depending on the involvement of individual units and commanders and who were behind this plot, a selection would be made as to who would be informed, rather those who were not involved than those who are. Therefore, such intelligence cannot be made public immediately, and everyone cannot be made aware of them straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've talked about this -- I think you called it perhaps a stumbling-block area where a security officer needs to decide if he has received information that he should tell his commander about or he shouldn't tell his commander about. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this is an extremely complex matter and that it is very hard to find the right degree in estimating what should be said at a given moment and what should not be said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this has to do with counter-intelligence information. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And you also said that -- I think something to the effect that when in doubt, it's best to inform your commander. Is that correct? Something like that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know how to answer that question. Depending on the context. I think that if we're talking about counter-intelligence, that the opposite would be true. If one has doubts, assumptions, some certain initial indications or suspicions, on the contrary, the commander should be spared at the outset because it could be counterproductive. We must be misinforming him; maybe nothing will come of it. If we're talking about counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we're talking about use of the military police or matters that may involve operational issues related to troops and movements, would the security officer inform his commander of that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not understand the question. Whose movement? What troops?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The movement of MPs to guard troops, for example. We're not in the counter-intelligence area any more. We're in the area of MP units guarding troops. Wouldn't that be something the security officer would inform his commander about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for such engagement of the military police, it is not the security organ who decides that that will be done. This has to be based on an order issued by the commander to the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. In any event, it is within a commander's responsibility to know what his military police are doing at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you also, you talked about internal threats to the security of a unit --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you if this example I'm giving you is an internal threat to a security of a unit. If prisoners within the custody of an army are systematically abused by the people guarding them, can that threaten the security and the safety of that army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a public matter. That does not fall under counter-intelligence information in the sense in which I mentioned it or in the sense in which it is treated by the rules of service and relevant laws. This is something that has to do with order, discipline, responsibility. Something that may constitute a threat in relation to the general security of the unit, but it cannot fall into the category of secret counter-intelligence information. One's superior officer always has to be aware of such information; that is to say, the commanding officer of the unit and also the person higher up in the chain of command. Everybody has to be informed about this, and everybody has to take measures with a view to resolving the problem. But it's a public matter, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. And I'm not asking about counter-intelligence. My question was, is such abuse, does that threaten the very security and safety of the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every excessive use of force may produce negative effects or may have a counter-effect. There can be a rebellion on the part of those who are being guarded. So this could become a serious security problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the opposing forces found out about such abuse, they could also inflict their own abuse, couldn't they? And that would affect the security of the army or the civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. It can cause a reaction and an appropriate response by the other side. Let's simplify matters: If one side abuses prisoners, then it is to be expected that by way of reciprocity, it will be done by the other side, too. From that point of view, I do agree with what you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And so like what you have said, it is a commander's duty; in fact, it's his imperative to know about such abuse and such threats for the morale, for the safety. He needs to know about that kind of thing, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've just seen Dragan Obrenovic acknowledging that he authorised the murder of thousands of people. When Dragan Obrenovic said that, he very simply acknowledged he was part of it, and he said he was part of the vortex of hatred that led to that. So on one hand we have a horrible situation of abuse of prisoners that could actually lead to terrible problems; and on the other hand, we have an organised system of killing prisoners because of the, according to Obrenovic, the vortex of hatred.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this because at this point in time now we're demonising the entire VRS and the entire Serb population by virtue of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I resent that kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, let Mr. Karnavas finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic may have his own opinions, but he cannot speak for the rest of the Serb people and the rest of the Serb army. He can speak about his conduct. Maybe he had the hatred and the dark heart and wanted to seek revenge on others. But he can't that everybody who was in the VRS, every soldier, every officer felt the same way. And so I think the question is rather broad. Now if he wants to narrow it, I don't have a problem. But the way it's phrased, I think it's overly broad. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the Prosecutor's question, if you see clearly there's a phrase saying that "according to Obrenovic." And I guess, you know, that is his view on that. I don't see that there's any blames on the whole population or the whole nationality for the crimes of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you read the entire question that when it goes on, Your Honour, he premises that. And then he goes on to frame it as if that is an acknowledged fact and that's where I disagree. Obrenovic may have those feelings, I don't have a problem. But then when he takes Obrenovic's position and adopts it as a holistic position for everyone else, I do object to that. Now, if he wants to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I cannot stand here and be defamed like that in front of the former Yugoslavia. I cannot. I have to speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's an overbroad question. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Well, Mr. McCloskey, basically speaking, I think there's no problem in your question, but it's not clear maybe to the others. Maybe you could have it somehow modified so that, you know, you do not give a wrong impression or do not let us to get a wrong impression of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hope you're not suggesting that I gave you the impression that I think all Serbs feel hatred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no. No, you did not. But we have to try our best to avoid this, you know, collective responsibility matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I am certainly not suggesting that all Serbs felt this, nor would I suggest that all American soldiers felt bad after the Mile massacre, or that all Americans felt it, or that all the forces currently at war feel that. But clearly we see throughout history horrible things done in a time of war, things that happen that people would never even dream of in peacetime. And I was just asking you if you could help us explain, if you know, how it is that such a terrible thing could happen where despite the internal security threat that that would pose on its own troops, despite the horrible effect on the people, the victims of the crime, that soldiers and officers could allow this to happen and take part in it. And you don't need to answer it if you can't.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot give an answer, but I did want to say that what happened certainly does constitute a flagrant violation of all sorts of rules of warfare, of humanitarian law, of human rights conventions. And there is something else I wished to say: A few minutes ago I talked about this commission that is now preparing its final report. We indeed do not have an answer yet to the question how this started and whose idea this was and who conceived of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In speaking of prisoners of war, in your testimony you emphasised I think the role of the rear services and how important it was for the assistant commander for rear services to be able to provide medical care, food, water, the essentials of the Geneva Conventions. And I'm sure you stand by that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say when this was abided by and when it was not abided by. But that is how the rules regulates it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's not just the assistant commander for rear services that has this responsibility for prisoners, is it? It's actually his -- the commander for the assistant. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This involves responsibility for all questions and all elements of functioning of a unit. That's what the commander's responsibility is. According to the rules of service and the laws, some of these rights are delegated to his assistant commanders. But generally speaking, it is the commander whose responsibility all of this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to the time frame that -- where you actually were on the ground in some of the areas where some things happened. And I just want to go briefly to Exhibit P113. And if we could show you P113B. This is this order that you said you never saw. And I want to try to get some clarity on the dates. We see that there's an incoming stamp, looks like it's from the command of the Milici Brigade. And it says, looks like 18 July. And I'm not sure we can really make out a time. But the document is dated 17 July, and it looks like Milici may have got it sometime on the 18th. So that would indicate that sometime late on the 17th, that this order was in force and in effect, or at least someone thought it was, and sent it off to the various units that it's addressed to. And those would be the Drina Corps command, the Zvornik Brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, the Milici Brigade, and the 67th Communications Regiment. Now, when we spoke to you in Banja Luka, you had told us that you went to the area on the 18th, and you told us that you had been able to check your diary. Have you been able to look at your diary before coming and testifying now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you permit me, at the very outset, I would like to say that not at any point in time did I say that I had never seen this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought you hadn't seen it. When did you first see it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you showed it to me in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, okay. I meant during the wartime you hadn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I did not see it. I really did say yesterday that I do not know on which day exactly I was in Bratunac, or rather, in that area. As far as I can remember, when I spoke to Mr. Ruez, I told him then, too, that I came to that date on the basis of some notes that I have which were simply in a notebook, not a proper war logbook. And I have an outline of the activities that were taking place during those days. I also said that I was in a dilemma, and I know that this is an order that was conveyed to me in the afternoon hours. And then bearing in mind when this reached the units involved, that is to say, the 17th of the afternoon, and you say that some units received this even on the 18th, on the basis of that and on the basis of those notes of mine, I inferred that it is more likely that it was the 18th. I really don't know which day it is. But now that I have seen other documents as well, I still cannot say with any degree of certitude that it is the 17th or the 18th, but it must be one of those two dates. That's for sure. And that's what I said yesterday at the very outset. I cannot say anything with any degree of certainty because I did not remember that day in terms of its date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I understand. My question is have you had a chance to review those notes that you had reviewed before you were spoken to in Banja Luka. If you recall, I think you've quoted us from those notes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This little notebook does exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you bring it with you by any chance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think you could provide us that notebook so we can copy it and send it back to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, it does not contain anything that would prevent me from handing it over to you. As a matter of fact, you can get in touch with the office in Banja Luka and they can have it photocopied straight away if you like, so you can see it any way you wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We probably should have asked you that a couple of years ago. All right. Now, you've told us that General Mladic modified that order after Tolimir talked him out of it because it was according to you and I guess Tolimir that this was not a reasonable order. So it was possible to talk Mladic over things that were unreasonable?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was unrealistic. I don't know whether I used the word "unreasonable." But Tolimir accepted it, and that is the position that he took to Mladic. It is true that at certain points in time -- or rather, not at certain points in time, always when somebody would try to suggest things to him reasonably or to explain things to him reasonably, General Mladic would change his decision in the sense of correct it or simply say, "All right, it doesn't have to be that way." That could happen. It did happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you went to the area on the 17th or perhaps the 18th, were you aware of about a hundred, 150 prisoners gathered in the area of Konjevic Polje or Lolici on the afternoon of the 17th or the morning of the 18th? They were put in, I believe, three buses or trucks.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know how many detainees or prisoners there were. But I did see and know that in Konjevic Polje there were vehicles that had been prepared, or rather brought there for the purpose of the evacuation or transport of detainees if necessary. I did see some buses and trucks as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you see detainees?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the -- your understanding, who was the person, the commander on the ground that was responsible for the sweep operations in the area of Kravica and Konjevic Polje at the time you went?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say who was in charge -- I mean, I cannot say who was in charge at the Kravica location but what I can say is what was said to me. That with -- regarding activities in that zone, the sweep-up operation, that that is the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, that he's in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who told you that Colonel Blagojevic was in charge of the sweep operation in that zone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command post at the Main Staff. General Mladic quite literally said, or perhaps I'm going to give an interpretation of what he said. Blagojevic organised a sweep of the terrain. It is moving along, but it is moving along slowly. It needs to be speeded up. You will go down there and you will have an overview of this, and you will speed things up. And Miletic is going to give you more specific tasks. That's my knowledge in this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you mean Miletic or Malinic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miletic. General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operations officer at the Main Staff. Head of the operations administration or whatever it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Chief of Staff around during this time period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The chief of the Main Staff? No. General Milovanovic? No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was somewhere out in the Krajina somewhere, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know roughly -- very roughly what period of time Milovanovic was out of the area of Han Pijesak and out in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that little notebook is going to help us because already from the 23rd or 24th of July, I joined him at the forward command post of the Main Staff in Drvar. And also before that, there may be some notes. I'm not sure about the period before that, but from that point in time onwards, I'm sure that he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, was there an acting Chief of Staff, deputy commander in Han Pijesak while Milovanovic was away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there was one officially. If you allow me, may I say that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's pretty simple. But go ahead. Go ahead. No, go ahead. If you need to explain, you can always explain.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to say that - and you probably have this information anyway - that the Main Staff involved such a small number of people that quite literally everybody did everything. So people could be replaced all the time. If one person was not there, then somebody else could take over for him. And people would have several duties. So it is possible that from that point of view somebody did stand in for General Milovanovic, but I'm not sure whether anybody was officially appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On those days, the 16th, 17th, 18th, who was basically in charge over there when Mladic wasn't around?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Miletic was the most senior-ranking officer as the operations officers. He would be the number three man on the staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And let's go to, I think, the area of Nova Kasaba. I think you have told us that you spoke to Malinic, and that Malinic talked to you about these 2000 or so prisoners that were at the soccer field on the 13th of July in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that Mladic had -- he told you that Mladic had given him an order to send them to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Mladic came by, stopped, gathered these people together, spoke to them, and said that they would be evacuated and that they would go home following their families who were passing along that road precisely at that time. Soon after that, buses and trucks came to that place. And these people were evacuated, or rather driven to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Apparently it's break time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll resume at 2.00 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, good afternoon. This shouldn't take too much longer. We were talking about your recollections of what Major Malinic was telling you when you saw him on the 13th of July in Nova Kasaba. Do you remember just roughly what time of day it was when you first saw him there in Nova Kasaba and he gave you some of this information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the middle of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Are there any problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's a misstatement. He never said that he saw him on the 13th. I believe it was on the 17th that he saw him, and the discussion was with respect to the events of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct. I apologise. He's absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we -- I think we all know that. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, General, that's, of course, what I meant to say. When you saw him on the 17th and about what he had told you what was going on, on the 13th. Now, do you remember -- did he tell you anything about Colonel Beara being in the area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a certain point in time, he or someone close to him mentioned Beara in the context of the prisoners from the 13th, that apparently he had passed on the order or ordered for them to be collected at the stadium in Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say "he had passed on the order," you mean Beara had passed on the order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Major Malinic or one of his -- someone close to him provided you that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Have you had a chance to look at your statement that you gave us in Banja Luka back in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just provide you a copy with it. There's just a couple of things I just want to ask you about that you mention there. And it should be on page 71 going over into page 72 in the B/C/S; and in the English, it should be 01907127. And Mr. Ruez asked you a question about what reports you received regarding Nova Kasaba on the 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th. And this is what you say: "I'm not sure if he told me on that occasion, but around that time during those days he said that on the part of the Kasaba-Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road, we captured a number of soldiers of the 28th Division or the persons from Srebrenica. And then I think he told me that Colonel Beara ordered that all of them should be gathered in the soccer field in Nova Kasaba." Now, at this point are you talking about Major Malinic, what Major Malinic is telling you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then to go on, he says: "In his assessment, because he didn't count them properly, around 2.500 people were gathered. He allegedly, because I didn't check it out, he allegedly started making lists of the arrested persons, but this was stopped by the arrival of General Mladic who gathered those people up and addressed them." Do you remember that? Did he tell you that the lists were -- about the lists?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I have already said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. "Allegedly, he told them that they would all be evacuated to where they wanted to go, toward Tuzla, because they had supposedly set off for Tuzla. After that, it must have been the 13th, according to Malinic, buses arrived in the area of Nova Kasaba, and that group was driven to Bratunac. And then in a number of places, those people were taken over by the troops of the Bratunac Brigade. There, he lost track of them, and I don't know what happened after that." Is that a fair statement of what Major Malinic told you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a correct statement regarding the fact that they were taken to Bratunac. I'm not sure now whether it is quite correct to say that they were taken over by the forces of the Bratunac Brigade. That's the only part I'm not quite sure about. Everything else stands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see your words written there on that paper or what should be your words?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not doubt the correctness of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was your memory back in 2000 better than it is today about these events and what was told to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory was certainly better, but my knowledge was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you did tell us that back in 2000. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you could now just go to page 79, it should be about lines 14 through 24. And in our English, it should be 01907135. And Mr. Ruez asked you one of his long questions about prisoners and ends it with: "Within the Bratunac Brigade, who is especially in charge of dealing with prisoners?" And your response is: "I am not sure that they were placed under the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, but they were taken to the area of the Bratunac Brigade, whether they were taken over by the Bratunac Brigade or civilian police or both. From a professional point of view, the chief of security of that brigade would be responsible for prisoners within the brigade's zone. But everything is within the responsibility of the commander." Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mean the commander of the brigade when you said that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the commander who is in control of the area of responsibility. Yes, one could say brigade commander in whose area of responsibility this was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, thank you very much. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any redirect, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Major Malinic these days; do you know, General?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. But I believe that Major Malinic is somewhere in Serbia, or rather the last time I had any information about him he was in Serbia in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just a couple of questions: Did he specifically tell you who ordered the men, the prisoners, to go to Bratunac? Who issued that order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me who issued the order. But he said that sometime after the commander of the Main Staff had addressed the people, buses and trucks appeared in the area of Nova Kasaba, that the prisoners were boarded on to and driven off to Bratunac. He didn't tell me who told them to go to Bratunac, or at least I don't remember him telling me. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever say anything about Colonel Blagojevic being handed over these prisoners, or being involved at all in these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. A minor detail that comes to mind from subsequent conversations is that there was no one there who could take over those prisoners and that during the night they allegedly stayed in the vehicles they were brought in, that the people guarded them or somebody from Bratunac outside the brigade. I learned that from a subsequent conversation. He never mentioned that he had handed them over to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say that -- did he ever say who handed over these prisoners to whomever? In other words, when they left, who accompanied these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, or rather I really don't know whether we discussed that. I am unable to answer that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand your testimony correct on direct, you were not around during that period of time, so you have no first-hand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Yes, your understanding is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Judge Argibay, please. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I have only one question. It's a clarification.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You told us that General Tolimir was the number four in the Main Staff, that General Miletic was number three, and we all know that General Mladic was number one. But I'm not sure from the transcript this morning, or yesterday, when you were talking about General Milovanovic, was he number two in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, General Milovanovic was the number two, but General Tolimir was not number four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: You said so, that Tolimir probably was number four.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember saying that. I think that I didn't give a number. He is one of the assistant commanders of the Main Staff, and there were five or six of them at the same level in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Could you give me more or less the order, then. More or less.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first three, what you said is quite right. Mladic, Milovanovic, and then Miletic. And then the assistants, according to their departments, come in the following: Tolimir, Gvero, Dukic, Tomic. I think those were the sectors represented at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Argibay. Any questions out of the Judge's questions? I see none. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a correction: I believe I referred to the 17 July document as P113. That was one of the earlier false numbers. It should have been P500. But I think it's...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. The usher will show you out of the room, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home. You may go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, concerning the next witness, I have some matters to discuss with the parties. And for the sake of the precaution, shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And after consultations with my colleagues, we'll lift the protective measures granted in the previous testimony. So there's no need for us to go into private session when we come across his testimony he gave previously. Yes, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps when Madam usher comes. I see I'm being assisted by the...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: By the way, is this the last witness for this week, or we have another witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the last witness, Your Honour. And if, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to use one-and-a-half hours for the direct examination? Because tomorrow, we have to sit in the afternoon. And tomorrow is a Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am always making my tactical and strategic decisions based on the moment. So we'll see how it goes. But I hope that we can accommodate everyone's afternoon tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Just one point about the exhibits we received this morning, the exhibit list, and we noted there are two exhibits on -- the two last ones, two books, translation pending. But we haven't received either book, so we don't know what it's all about. And it's very difficult for us obviously to prepare for these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I just received that list. Mr. Karnavas, would you please give us an explanation on that. If without translation, how could we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there are always ways, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Give me your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In anticipation, the gentleman came with two books. We're having the entire books copied for the Prosecution so they can add it to their collection. And the significant portions of them -- the one has been translated. It's only one paragraph. It deals with the concept of all people's defence. That's an unofficial translation that we provided, that we did, although the official one is pending. With respect to the other one, there are about five or six pages. The translation is pending, but the gentleman is going to be making reference to portions from those pages. We provided copies to the translators. He's going to be reading rather slow. It really isn't anything earth-shattering. It basically deals with the whole concept of commanding. And we apologise, but this was brought to our attention last night, late last night might I add. So our thoughts were to allow the gentleman to speak. He can make reference. I'm going to ask him if he has consulted any or looked at any books, can these theories that he's telling us contained in any books. And of course he will say yes. He will speak in general, and then that material will eventually - all of it - be made available to the Prosecution. The entire text, not just the sections. I don't have a problem in not introducing those documents. I'm certainly going to ask the gentleman who has studied what books are generally referred to or used. And so it's the Prosecution that continually objects not to having these books available to them. I'm making the opportunity available to them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's just not according to the Rules that we are not even given these -- I'm not even talking about translations. We don't have it. And while I think it's great that the interpreters have copies, I think that's wonderful, but we need to have it, and not just when it starts but sometime ago. They could have faxed it last night if they realised it last night that he came with something. We simply don't have anything, and I think that's not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And just now you mentioned that you have certain paragraphs translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you furnish it to the other party?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They should have been, Your Honour. Of course, the case manager was working past midnight as I understand. The one page, the one book which is called "Strategy of Armed Combat," it's literally the introduction, one paragraph, they should have it. It's supposed to be D200/1. It doesn't take a whole lot to read that. The second one is from the introduction to "The Theory of Military Management," by Mr. Branislav Jovanovic. This is D201. And again, I can work around this. I can merely say, "Are there any texts," and not introduce anything, and -- but he can certainly discuss the theories of this. Mind you that this witness was a Prosecution witness. The Prosecution had available this witness to question him about commanding. Now, the other document is a manual for the work of commanders and staff, one which we received from the Prosecution. Where this becomes relevant, all of this, is as you recall in the cross-examination of Butler, one, he noted that he was not unfamiliar with the specifics of the concept of all people's defence. Secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. We're getting into policy and Butler and arguments, and this is way beyond where this should be going. And I just want to point out that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who is doing the cross-examination, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think at this stage, I just want you to explain why we don't have the translation and how could we proceed without the translation? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I tried to give an explanation, and then I went a little further so we can have context. And I would appreciate if you would interrupt me, Your Honour. I don't mind that. But for the Prosecution to just simply interrupt because they feel they have nothing better to do, I do get upset about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I unfortunately will have to continue to interrupt where we go off into the argument of his case and the criticism of Mr. Butler. But to try to make things easy, if it's just the introduction and there's not too many references, maybe we can just see how we go and -- I just hope it won't happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's very cooperative. And we'll go with those documents, but we have to remind the Defence counsel that in the future whenever they want to use a document, especially in the direct examination, you have to provide copies to the other parties and have the proper translation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I agree. And I don't want to make an issue of, this but this particular week has been very challenging for us, especially with the Court scheduling that we've had to accommodate everyone else, including Madam Del Ponte. So, you know, I'm doing my best. I learned of it late last night, as I think the Trial Chamber knows, I try to be diligent. I don't like having to be here to listen to these objections, and I don't really object to their objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think they're legitimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
