utterances.text: Yes, let's have the witness. Let's have the witness, please. And before that, could we make sure that you furnish the copies to the translation booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe they have been, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have any documents whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could ask Madam Usher to furnish them with the copies if you have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You are not going to use it at this moment, right? Maybe for the next sitting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was hoping that we could just -- you know, I was going to do a tactical approach to this and be as efficient as possible in light of tomorrow being Friday and an afternoon sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We do have copies, Your Honour. And it would only take 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry for keeping you waiting outside because, you know, there are a lot of matters that have to be solved. And would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, and let me apologise for being the cause of this delay, or at least part of the cause. Could you please tell us your name, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Mirko Trivic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record, could you tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: My last name is T-r-i-v-i-c, C with a diacritic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trivic. Could you please tell us a little bit about your educational background.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Military or general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll start from the general, and then we're going to get into the military.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Before the military academy, I completed high school, general high school, of course. Then I completed the military academy in 1971. Then the Command Staff Academy. And postgraduate studies in wartime skills.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And first of all, your postgraduate studies, how long is that? How many years?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: It lasted two years. Just before the breakup of Yugoslavia and before the war started, in 1992 I defended the project I worked on. That was actually my master's degree. And it was accepted as such, and then I was supposed to defend it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in total, how many years do you have in military education?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: As for my military education, I spent four years at the military academy, one year at the command and staff academy, two years doing my postgraduate course, and one year approximately at different advanced courses in order to keep abreast of the technical development and the development of the overall concept of all people's defence. So it's a total of eight years very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us how many years -- how many years of field experience you have in the military.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from the academy, until completing my postgraduate course, I worked for 17 years in the field, in the troops. And then after the -- after I got my master's degree, I worked in the system of higher military education. And then from the war until the year 2000, that is to say, from 1993 until the year 2000, once again, I worked in operative units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the rank -- your highest -- well, currently are you in the military?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No. Not now. I'm not in the military now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what rank did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: The rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during those years, have you had an opportunity to teach military -- at any military institutions?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The department of tactics at the military academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that at the entrance level of cadets going to the academy?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What level --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: No. This is general for the military academy and for courses that were organised at the military academy for other schools as well. There was a post-secondary education for NCOs who wanted to get further training, et cetera. And then also at the Faculty of National Defence for students of national defence. And at other institutions that were factors in the system of all people's defence, like the MUP, or the police, rather, and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, since you mentioned already all people's defence, I would like to start there. And first of all, let me ask, do you feel competent enough to discuss this concept of all people's defence? Do you feel you have the educational background, the military experience to discuss this topic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I think I can take part in discussions and reach conclusions on the basis of the theory I know and the practice I went through. I can reach appropriate conclusions with regard to relevant facts, and all of this has to do with the further advancement of war skills and practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, so we can understand what this concept is, let me first ask you, would you call the all people's defence a military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: When speaking of all people's defence, a distinction has to be made between two things: On the one hand, the concept of all people's defence, which constitutes a sociopolitical and military strategic idea, concerning the preparation and organisation of a society, a system, a state, in relation to its defence from potential aggressors. On the other hand, from this concept, from this sociopolitical and military strategic idea, the doctrine of all people's defence is derived. And it spells out in more concrete terms the concept itself, and it is based on science, military science, and science in general in terms of control and command aimed at the realisation of this concept. From both comes the strategy which means the implementation of all of this in an armed struggle, and it guides all factors in society how they will participate in a general conflict. And then the rules of conduct are based on this strategy that is pursued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would it -- if I understand part of -- the latter portion of your answer, could you please tell us whether the rules for the military, the rules, the laws, the regulations upon which the military relies on, are they based in part on this concept of all people's defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, a concept and a doctrine, if the doctrine is spelled out in concrete terms in that way, they necessitate the adoption of laws in terms of how all subjects will act in case of war. So laws on their responsibilities are based on that. And also, for the special forces that lead the armed struggle, there have to be rules of conduct through strategy. But that also has to be within the framework of the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, I want to show you what has been marked for identification purposes as D200/1. If we could put the English version on the ELMO, and if you could just look at it. First of all, let me just ask you, I'm holding a book in my hands, a red book. And the copies that you have, is that from this particular book that I'm holding?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I could get you to look at the introduction part, and that would be... First, I want to just read it out and you can follow along. And then I would like to discuss this in some part. It states here: "The strategy of armed combat is theory in practice in the preparation in carrying out of armed combat as a whole in the all people's defence war and the highest branch of war skills. It is formed on the concept and doctrine of all people's defence, and social self-protection which comes forth out of the socialist self-governing social order a neutral foreign politics and experience in people's liberation wars. The main points of the conception are entailed in the SFRJ constitution, the programme and congress documentation of the Union of Communists of Yugoslavia, the law on all people's defence, and the directives for the defence of the SFRJ from aggression. A strategy of armed combat is consistently taken from them, imposes their application and elaboration in the domain of armed combat in an all people's defensive war." Is this not the introduction from this particular book that I've shown you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this text a text that is used or that is -- that is used by the military?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we see the date. That's 1983. So this would have been for the JNA in the former Yugoslavia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to now fast forward to 1992 and onwards in the VRS. Was the concept that we just read in the introduction applicable at that time for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: This concept was applicable for the Army of Republika Srpska. Unfortunately, it was actually supposed to be applicable to all peoples as they left the joint state. But all mobilisation decisions were based on it concerning mobilisation of units for defence, not only in relation to an aggression coming from the outside; that is to say, from an external aggressor, but also when attempts were made to try to start a war among different ethnic groups within the country. But it was not only applicable, but it was actually applied. And it was carried through, especially in reference to the law on all people's defence which governs the system of all people's defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you: Concretely, could you please tell us how this concept of all people's defence works. Just if you had to describe it to a foreigner, how would you describe it but in a very concrete manner?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that all of this resulted in a law on all people's defence. That is to say, both the concept and the doctrine resulted in that. They're both regulated by law and are binding on all subjects and forces of the state and society to take part in an all people's defensive war. The forces as stipulated by law were all the working people and citizens of the state, all the nations and nationalities of the country, all sociopolitical communities at all levels, from the very lowest cell, namely, the local commune, and then through the municipality and republics and provinces all the way up to the federation, then all sociopolitical organisations that were headed by the League of Communists as this ideological force within the system, and the others that can also be enumerated. That is to say, all the cells of the society, all human and material potentials that these subjects have. Especially with regard to waging an all-out armed struggle, it was the duty of all on the basis of the law on national defence to organise special forces that will take part in the decisive factor of resisting the aggressor, and that is to say, a defensive war if a war were to happen. So those were the armed forces. The civilian defence, the observation and reporting system, those were the forces that were stipulated as such. When all of this is viewed and when all of this is laid as a foundation, then in this way the following conclusion can be reached, that no one in the state was excluded, neither an individual or collective or an organisation of associated labour as they were called then, work organisations and so on. Everybody had their own obligations and responsibilities. And they carried them out in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. I understand -- well, I have a difficulty, you know, to your approach to direct examine this witness. This Tribunal is a Tribunal, not a military academy. We spend a lot of time in those obstructive concepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I hope that maybe you could take incidents or take documents if they mention all people's defence and the parties have some different views on it, you could ask some questions to this witness, rather than lay down such a profound background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It should be case oriented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. That was going to be my very next question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just quote from the record of Richard Butler. Cross-examination. He's being asked, and this can be found on page 4.789. We have it for the ELMO. And for the record actually, you can go back further than I'm reading. But I'm going to start at line 22. For your information, Mr. Trivic, Mr. Butler was an OTP analyst, employee. Line 22, he's asked: "When you say all people's defence, that would be what you would consider the doctrine for the former Yugoslavia?" Answer: "Yes, sir." Question: "Okay. And I take it that would apply to Bosnia-Herzegovina at this particular time frame?" Answer: "The -- well, for -- I assume for 1995, with respect to the VRS, they were implementing the JNA basis of the regulations. Whether or not on a broader level they were encompassing all the principles of all people's defence, I don't know. But certainly, where they would use it in the conduct of their military campaigns and in the content -- conduct of their general military strategy, they did so. It was all they had." Question: "And I take it you're familiar with the all people's defence?" Answer: "At a very broad level. Not at the specific, sir." "Did you know of its applicability prior to the war in 1992?" Answer: "Not in detail, sir, no, sir." And then I comment: "Well, I guess we'll skip that part of the discussion." Now, sir, an analyst who is trying to understand the VRS at that point in time, 1995, in light of reading rules and regulations of the VRS military that were actually JNA, and of course, other material, my question is how significant would it be for an analyst to really thoroughly understand and appreciate the doctrine of all people's defence?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO TRIVIC
utterances.text: I think that a good analyst must know the bases from which the rules of service were developed, the way in which an army is organised, under wartime conditions. Because it was the underlying basis for the organisation of the army, and that system was applied in organising the army. That is why it is necessary to have a full understanding of that organisation to know what its sources are, to be able to make qualified conclusions regarding the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you, you know, had Mr. Butler consulted you or asked you about the concept or military doctrine of all people's defence, had he been interested, would he -- would you have been willing to explain it to him thoroughly so he would fully understand it and know how it should be applied in relation to understanding the rules and regulations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Objection. That's entirely inappropriate to ask this witness. And the question is entirely full of remarks about Mr. Butler, "trying to understand" and so on. I think that's not help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may respond very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was a reason why I framed the question in such a manner, because there was also a very good reason why I asked Mr. Butler on cross-examination had he consulted with any JNA officers, be they from Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, anywhere outside the conflict, not necessarily Serbs. utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Here he has mentioned if we had access. Just again to remind, not in the 65 ter summary or anywhere else was it mentioned that the Butler report would be discussed, the all people's defence will be discussed. I think it's impossible to prepare for an entirely new field with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, that's incorrect. I have been giving them messages left and right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, first of all, the question you asked is a hypothetical question. Secondly, I don't think it's relevant to the case in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thirdly, you still did not establish any links between the concept of all people's defence to our very case. This is what we want to hear. I think I give you some directions. If you have some documents we have already admitted that comment on this concept, you may ask some questions which should not be within the academic circles, but should be realistic, you know, closely related to our case, to your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. If I may respond very briefly, and with all due respect, we had five days of Butler direct examination. It was a long week, as you may recall. utterances.text: At this moment, good. All right. Your Honour, I'm used to going from the general to the specific, and I'm going to be going more specific from now on.

utterances.text: Yes. The witness is not the first time to be a witness in this Trial Chamber, so shall we come to specific documents, specific orders. If they are mentioned, some commander's relationship, zone of defence, you know, you could ask some questions.

utterances.text: I can restructure my direct, Your Honour, if you wish for me to go into a particular topic at this point and discuss this map. I could do that. utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the difference between us is just our approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I agree.
